analysis.one_liner: Stops medical debt from appearing on credit reports and bars lenders from using it.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 29, 2025 with 17 Democratic cosponsors, the bill has sat in the House Financial Services Committee without a vote since the day it was referred.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal credit-reporting law so that medical debt — including bills sent to collections — can never appear on a person's credit report. It would also require the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write rules barring lenders from looking at someone's medical debt when deciding whether to lend to them. The goal is to keep an illness or injury from wrecking a person's credit score and cutting off access to loans, housing, and jobs that check credit.
analysis.who_benefits: People who have medical debt would gain the most. Under the bill, an unpaid hospital bill or a bill sent to a collection agency could no longer be reported to credit bureaus, so getting sick would no longer drag down a credit score [S2]. Because credit scores affect mortgages, car loans, credit cards, apartment rentals, and sometimes employment screening, removing medical debt from reports would protect people's access to all of these after a medical event [S2]. Lenders would be barred from using medical debt information in credit decisions within one year of enactment, with the consumer bureau required to rewrite its regulations [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with medical debt on their credit

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act to exclude any adverse information related to medical debt from consumer reports, explicitly including debt that was placed for collection or charged off — closing the current exception that allows collected medical debt to be reported
Defines medical debt broadly as any debt arising from the receipt of medical services, products, or devices, so the protection covers the full range of health care bills

Requires the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, within one year of enactment, to change its regulations so creditors are prohibited from obtaining or using medical debt information when deciding whether to extend credit

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies and medical debt collection firms lose a product and a collection tool: credit bureaus could no longer sell files containing medical debt, and collectors could no longer use the threat of credit damage to pressure people into paying. Some lenders lose a data point some of them use in underwriting, and if medical debt does correlate with repayment risk, lenders would absorb that risk in their pricing. Nothing in the bill erases the underlying debt, so hospitals and providers are still owed what they are owed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and medical debt collectors

drawbacks.text: The bill does not reduce or forgive any debt. People would still owe the medical bills, still face collection calls and lawsuits over them; the bill only hides the debt from credit reports and from lender underwriting

Because the bill bars creditors from using medical debt information in credit decisions, lenders can no longer distinguish borrowers whose repayment trouble stems from a one-time medical event from those with broader financial distress, which an honest supporter would acknowledge could make credit pricing less precise or push some risk costs onto other borrowers

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: a medical emergency would no longer follow someone through their credit file for years and block them from housing, cars, or credit. The cost falls on credit bureaus and collection firms, plus some loss of underwriting information for lenders — a reasonable trade if the alternative is punishing people for getting sick. The main design weakness is that the bill treats the symptom, not the cause: the debt itself remains, and the bill does nothing about medical billing, insurance gaps, or the prices that produce the debt in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since; with Congress still in session, it remains technically alive but has not moved.

narrative.text: Rep. Nikema Williams introduced the Medical Debt Relief Act of 2025 in the House on July 29, 2025, with a group of original cosponsors including Reps. Correa, Krishnamoorthi, Scanlon, Kennedy of New York, Garcia of Illinois, Thompson, Pocan, Mullin, and Thanedar
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, the committee with jurisdiction over credit reporting law
The cosponsor list stands at 17, all Democrats; no Republican has signed on and no further action beyond the committee referral appears in the record

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, credit bureaus and medical debt collectors are better off, because the current rules that let medical debt appear on credit reports remain in place while the bill sits without action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus and medical debt collectors, for now

for.name: Rep. Nikema Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medical Debt Relief Act of 2025 and recruited the original cosponsors

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for any committee action since it was referred on July 29, 2025

sides.party_line_note: All 18 supporters in the record — the sponsor and 17 cosponsors — are House Democrats, and no Republican has cosponsored or otherwise acted on the bill.

industries.note: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion would be barred from including any medical debt — including collected medical debt — in the consumer reports they sell. Medical debt has been a steady stream of file entries and dispute volume, and removing it takes away a reason consumers need to buy credit monitoring and score products.

industries.industry: Debt collectors, especially medical debt buyers
industries.note: Collectors lose their most powerful lever: the threat of credit damage. The bill explicitly excludes medical debt placed for collection, so reporting would no longer be available to pressure payment, which would weaken the market for buying medical debt portfolios.

Lenders would be barred from obtaining or using medical debt information in credit decisions, removing a data point some use in underwriting while sparing lenders the hassle of medical coding questions on applications. Any added repayment risk would flow back into lending costs.

Providers remain entitled to collect what patients owe, but the softer collections environment and the loss of credit-report leverage could slow recovery of unpaid bills, even as patients get protection from credit ruin.

analysis.trajectory: With Republican control of the House and the Financial Services Committee, and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is likely to sit without a markup or hearing for the rest of the 119th Congress, much as prior versions of a medical-debt reporting ban stalled in committee in earlier Congresses. It would need a committee vote and floor action to have any chance of becoming law before the session ends January 3, 2027.
